# Lynas plans Brazil rare earths plant with state support

[Gabriel García](/external-author?external_author=Gabriel García) | October 12, 2026 | 5:45 am  [Critical Minerals](https://www.mining.com/category/critical-minerals/) [Intelligence](https://www.mining.com/category/intelligence/) [Top Companies](https://www.mining.com/category/top-companies/) [Australia](https://www.mining.com/region/australia/) [Latin America](https://www.mining.com/region/latin-america/) [Rare Earth](https://www.mining.com/commodity/rare-earth/)

![Lynas plans Brazil rare earths plant with state support](https://www.mining.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/caldeira.png)

Caldeira rare earth project location. (*Image courtesy of [Meteoric Resources | Facebook.](https://www.facebook.com/meteoricresources/)*)

Lynas Rare Earths (ASX: LYC) has presented plans to build a rare earth oxide separation plant in Brazil’s Minas Gerais state, Mines and Energy Minister Alexandre Silveira told MINING.COM, as the government considers backing a project that could become one of the largest such facilities outside China.

The proposal forms part of Lynas’ expansion into Brazil through its [$672 million acquisition of Meteoric Resources](https://www.mining.com/web/gina-rinehart-backed-lynas-to-buy-rare-earths-miner-meteoric/), whose Caldeira project hosts one of the world’s largest known ionic-clay rare earth deposits outside China. State development bank BNDES is evaluating potential financing, according to people familiar with the discussions.

“The project to implement a rare earth oxide separation plant in the Poços de Caldas region, presented by the company, could be a milestone for Brazil to advance through different stages of the value chain, adding value to our product and moving the country away from being merely an exporter of raw materials,” Silveira said in written comments.

The proposed facility would give Brazil a foothold in commercial-scale rare earth separation, an industry dominated by China, while potentially creating processing capacity for other ionic-clay deposits being developed in southern Minas Gerais.

## **Regional processing hub**

People familiar with the discussions told MINING.COM that negotiations are more advanced than Lynas’ public disclosures suggest, with a preliminary understanding around establishing separation capacity in Brazil.

BNDES is expected to conduct a technical visit to Lynas’ Australian operations before the end of 2026 as discussions progress. The financing structure and final investment decision remain undetermined.

Lynas had not responded to MINING.COM’s questions by publication time.

Government officials see the Poços de Caldas region as a potential processing centre for several nearby ionic-adsorption clay projects, allowing the proposed plant to handle material beyond Caldeira, according to people familiar with the discussions.

Such a facility could complement Lynas’ existing operations in Australia and Malaysia while establishing a downstream presence closer to South America’s emerging rare earth resources.
